newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Summit faces problem on Russia's place in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Summit faces problem on Russia's place in Europe.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
A European security summit next month will set a course for cooperation in the 21st century, with ringing declarations that the divisions of the Cold War are a thing of the past.

But, beneath the smooth diplomatic surface, the meeting of more than 50 countries in Lisbon has to tackle a serious problem -- how to make Russia feel that it is welcome and that NATO's plans to take in new members are not a threat to Moscow.

The last time the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) held a summit, in Budapest two years ago, the meeting was wrecked by rows over the war in Bosnia and Russian warnings that the whole continent faced renewed confrontation.

Since then, the Vienna-based body has shaken off the image of a worthy but ineffectual talking-shop, helped by the end of the Bosnia war a year ago and by a clearer picture of how security in Europe is to be managed in the post-Cold War world.

With a small staff and budget, it has organised difficult elections and arms control in Bosnia, helped broker ceasefires in Chechnya, monitored elections in Albania and won much credit for its particular brand of quiet diplomacy elsewhere.

Bringing together the United States and Canada with Russia and all other European states, it is increasingly seen as the best and most inclusive forum for dealing with issues of democracy, human rights and arms control.
"The Bosnia experience has certainly proved that we can play an effective role in European security," OSCE Secretary-General Giancarlo Aragona, an Italian, told Reuters.
"By and large, it's been successful. I sense that the system...is slowly becoming a reality. We are moving from the abstract to reality."

Peacekeeping, once agreed as a job for the OSCE in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict, is no longer high on the agenda since it has become clear that NATO is best suited to tackling hardcore military issues.
Nevertheless, the Lisbon summit on December 2 and 3 will not be all plain sailing.

Although many European leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac, will be there, neither Russian President Boris Yeltsin -- recovering from heart surgery -- nor U.S. President Bill Clinton are coming.

Russia, deeply suspicious of NATO's plans to expand into Eastern Europe and fearing isolation, has been trying to win agreement in Vienna for measures that would strengthen the OSCE and give it a leading role in European security issues.

Although NATO has agreed to build a special relationship with Russia, there is no chance Moscow will be able to join it. So Russia is keen to expand the influence and power of an organisation where it is a full member.

Moscow wants the OSCE to have a "steering group" of powerful members, modelled on the U.N. Security Council, which would guide Europe. It also wants the organisation to be given more legal authority, as a counterbalance to NATO.
Most other countries have rejected the proposals, although Germany and France have been urging their partners to show more flexibility and sympathy for Russian concerns.

Smaller nations do not want to lose their voice to a powerful "inner core" nor drop the principle that every country should have an equal voice, while Moscow's former satellites and most NATO nations remain suspicious of Russian motives.

Western diplomats agree that Russia needs to take something from the Lisbon summit that will show it has an important role in European security, but they say there is no chance that Moscow's proposals will be accepted.
Without much to show for its efforts, other than general declarations on the need for peace and cooperation, Russia could take a stronger line against NATO expansion.
By the middle of next year, the 16-nation alliance is expected to name the first countries to be admitted -- probably Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia.
"Time is running out," said a European diplomat in Vienna. "These processes are all linked to each other and it's very hard to see how we can satisfy the Russians."
Diplomats say Russia, which will be represented in Lisbon by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, hardened its position in preparatory talks this month in Vienna.

"They are trying to make sure that nothing in the Lisbon summit documents gives NATO any kind of approval for enlargement," said another diplomat. "If they can't get what they're after, they're going to play a blocking game."

Following the September elections in Bosnia, the summit is also expected to approve a continued role for the OSCE in Bosnia over the next two years, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force to make sure the fragile peace takes root.
Municipal elections in Bosnia have been postponed and diplomats say the European security body has a vital role to play in ensuring they finally go ahead next year.
But there is still some debate about the OSCE's exact role and problems with getting arms control agreements for former Yugoslavia, signed earlier this year, implemented.

Bosnia's three-man presidency, headed by Alija Izetbegovic, is expected to attend the Lisbon summit. Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic will not be there since Serbia and Montenegro were suspended from the OSCE during the war.

Other crises like the turmoil in Belarus will also be discussed. But the Lisbon summit will be, in part, a celebration of the progress made by an organisation that has its roots in the Cold War conflict 20 years ago.
The Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE) was set up in Helsinki in 1975 as an East-West forum for discussion of issues from human rights to economics.
Few believed at the time that it would be a useful body, since it could take decisions only if all members on both sides of the Iron Curtain agreed.

But it won a new lease of life after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, with the prospect of real security cooperation across Europe. At the Budapest summit two years ago, the name was changed to reflect these new hopes -- and it became the OSCE.
